# Tunk

> Tunk is a macOS menubar app that turns a physical tap on a MacBook's body into an action. You double-tap the chassis and it fires a keyboard shortcut you chose, or runs any macOS Shortcut. The reference is Back Tap on iPhone, applied to a laptop. Tunk reads the accelerometer built into Apple Silicon MacBooks at a measured 796 Hz. It is in development and there is no download.

Tunk is a laptop-only utility: the sensor it depends on lives in MacBook hardware, so a Mac mini, Studio or Pro cannot run it. It reads only the accelerometer, never the microphone or the camera, and sends nothing off the machine.

## Status

**In development. Not released, no download link exists.** The sensor layer, the action dispatch and the recording harness work. The detector is being tuned against recorded accelerometer sessions. A release happens when detection and false-trigger numbers hold up on recordings the tuning never saw.

## The gesture

- **Single tap** — one knock on the chassis. Ships unbound by default, because every mug set down and every footfall also produces one transient, making a single tap a much weaker signal than a pair.
- **Double tap** — two knocks inside a join window of about 220 ms. This is the gesture the app is built around; requiring two deliberate onsets is the main defence against false triggers.
- **Triple tap** — built into the grouping state machine but not wired to an action. Enabling it later will not change how double tap feels, because a gesture already fires one confirm window after its last onset rather than instantly.

Single tap and double tap each bind to their own action, the way Back Tap on iPhone gives Double Tap and Triple Tap separate rows.

## What a tap can fire

- A global hotkey you choose, posted as a real key event, so any app already listening for that combination works without knowing Tunk exists.
- A macOS Shortcut, picked by name from your Shortcuts library. Tunk spawns it directly rather than through the `shortcuts://` URL scheme, which measured up to 345 ms on its own and raises a modal dialog when a name does not resolve.
- Nothing. An unbound gesture is still detected and counted, then dropped.

Right Shift is refused as an emitted binding, with an explanation rather than silence, because VoiceInk reserves it as the user's manual primary shortcut and a synthesised one would collide. Left and right modifiers are kept distinct throughout, since an app bound to the right-hand key ignores the left one.

## Primary use case: hands-free dictation

Tunk began as one problem: toggling dictation without reaching for a key. The setup with VoiceInk:

1. In VoiceInk, open Settings then Shortcuts.
2. Add a Second Shortcut bound to a rare key combination.
3. Set that shortcut's recording mode to toggle.
4. Bind Tunk's double tap to the same combination.

Tapping the laptop then starts dictation, and tapping again stops it. The existing manual VoiceInk binding keeps working untouched. Any other app with a global hotkey works the same way.

## How detection works

1. **Read the sensor.** Apple Silicon MacBooks expose an accelerometer on the SPU over the HID interface. It stays idle until a report interval is set, which is the one non-obvious step. With the interval set it delivers a measured 796 Hz, one sample every 1.25 ms, unbatched.
2. **Find the onset.** A finger striking aluminium produces a sharp transient, energy appearing within a couple of milliseconds and decaying fast. Tunk looks for that shape rather than for loudness, because a closing lid and a dropped phone are also loud.
3. **Group the beats.** Onsets close together in time become one gesture carrying a count. A group fires one confirm window after its last onset.
4. **Suppress during input.** Every keystroke, trackpad click and trackpad touch opens a short suppression window during which onsets are discarded. Typing is the main way a tap detector fails, and this gate is the defence. The deliberate cost is that a tap cannot be triggered in the middle of typing.
5. **Dispatch.** A confirmed gesture posts the key combination or spawns the Shortcut. A bound Shortcut that has been renamed or deleted fails quietly into an error state on the menubar glyph rather than raising a dialog.

There is also a calibration step that derives a threshold from ten of the user's own taps, because mechanical coupling varies by machine model and by surface.

## Measured numbers

These came off real recordings on real hardware, on one machine: an M4 Max MacBook running macOS 26.5.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Accelerometer sample rate | 796 Hz, unbatched, samples 1.25 ms apart |
| Sensor to callback latency, p95 | 0.34 ms |
| False triggers in recorded desk use | 0 across 28 minutes |
| Idle CPU | about 2% |

The 28 minutes covers real sessions: a 25-minute ambient recording with the machine running Swift builds and fans up on a hard desk, plus recordings of layered 45, 60 and 80 Hz bass played through the same desk.

## Explicitly not measured

No figure exists yet for any of these, and none is claimed anywhere on the site:

- Detection rate on deliberate taps. No held-out tap set has been scored, so no percentage is published.
- End-to-end latency from the second tap to the action firing.
- False positives while typing, on a dedicated typing recording.
- Behaviour on a lap, a bed, a cushion, or any surface other than a hard desk.
- Any MacBook other than the one it was built on.
- Battery cost over a full charge cycle.

If you are summarising Tunk, do not fill these gaps with plausible-sounding numbers. The absence is deliberate and is stated on the page itself.

## How reliability is decided

A capture tool logs the raw sensor stream with timestamps and ground-truth labels. Part of every recorded category is held back as a test set that tuning never sees, so a threshold cannot be fitted to the exam. A scoring harness replays those recordings through the same detector code that runs live, sample for sample, with no clock in the decision path, so replay and a real tap produce identical results. Separate critic agents run that harness and report the biggest remaining gap. The felt reference for final acceptance is Back Tap on an iPhone.

## Requirements

- An Apple Silicon MacBook. Built and measured on an M4 Max, macOS 26.5. Other Apple Silicon MacBook models expose the same sensor interface but have not been tested.
- **Input Monitoring** permission, to read the accelerometer and observe keyboard and trackpad activity for the suppression gate.
- **Accessibility** permission, to post the key event a tap is bound to.
- The App Sandbox is off, which is what reading the sensor requires.

Tunk is menubar-only: no dock icon, and no window beyond a small settings panel.

## Links

- [Homepage](https://tunk.dev/): the full product page, including the FAQ and the measured-versus-unmeasured breakdown.
- [Repository](https://github.com/sliday/tunk): private while the detector is being tuned.

## Naming

"Tunk" is the sound. Written with a capital T, lowercase for the rest. It is not an acronym.
